blocks.content: Though the Indian Constitution is federal and envisages a dual polity, it provides for only a single citizenship, that is, the Indian citizenship.

rows: Single allegiance to the Union of India
Dual allegiance to the National Government and State
Uniform rights throughout the national territory
Different rights and privileges varying by State

items: Only Parliament—and NOT state legislatures—has the power to prescribe residence qualifications for employment under Article 16(3).
Residence is not listed as a forbidden ground of discrimination under Article 15; state governments can offer concessions (like educational fees) to state residents.
Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholders are not full citizens and do not enjoy voting rights or the right to hold constitutional offices.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Indian Constitution envisages a dual polity (Centre and States) but provides for only a single citizenship for the whole of India.
Unlike the USA, where a person is a citizen of both the USA and a specific state, Indian citizens owe allegiance only to the Union.
Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, but does not explicitly prohibit discrimination based on residence.
Under Article 16(3), Parliament alone can prescribe residence within a state or union territory as a condition for certain public employments.
Rights of non-tribals to move freely or settle in tribal areas can be restricted under Article 19 to protect the distinct culture and property of Scheduled Tribes.
